title: The Hub & Getting Started
description: The Hugging Face Hub as a registry, the Auto* classes for loading models, pipelines for fast prototyping, and how to read a model card before trusting a model.

lessons.title: What the Hugging Face Hub Is
lessons.description: Understand the Hub as a git-backed registry of models, datasets, and demos.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what the Hugging Face Hub stores and why a repo id like `bert-base-uncased` or `meta-llama/Llama-3-8B` is the thing you actually need to remember.

sections.title: 🗂️ A git host for machine learning artifacts
sections.content:
The **Hugging Face Hub** is a registry, built on git, that hosts three kinds of repos: **models** (trained weights and configs), **datasets** (data files plus loading scripts), and **Spaces** (small hosted demo apps). Every repo has an id in the form `org/name` — for example `google-bert/bert-base-uncased` or `openai/whisper-small`.

This is the same BERT and GPT-style architectures you studied in the transformers course, just packaged as downloadable, versioned artifacts instead of research-paper diagrams.

sections.title: 📄 The model card is the contract
sections.content:
Every model repo has a **model card** — a README describing what the model was trained on, its intended use, known limitations, and its **license**. Stars and download counts are popularity signals, not guarantees of quality or legal safety.

```python
# Conceptual: what you check before using a model
repo_id = "google-bert/bert-base-uncased"
# 1. What was it trained on?
# 2. What license governs reuse?
# 3. What are its documented limitations?
```

If you cannot name the repo id and its license, you cannot reproduce your own result later or answer a legal question about it.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating star count as a quality signal.** A popular repo can still be outdated or mismatched to your task — read the model card.

**Ignoring the license.** Some models are research-only or have usage restrictions; check before shipping a product on top of one.

**Not pinning a version.** The Hub keeps a commit history like git — pin a revision so your pipeline doesn't silently change when someone updates the repo.

questions.question: What does a Hugging Face Hub repo id like `google-bert/bert-base-uncased` identify?
options: A random tracking number with no meaning
The organization (or user) and the specific model repo within the Hub's git-backed registry
Only the license type of the model
The programming language the model was written in
questions.explanation: A repo id is `org/name` — it identifies exactly which organization or user published the repo and which model/dataset/Space it is, the same way a package name identifies a library.

questions.question: Why does a model's star count NOT tell you whether it's right for your task?
options: Stars are actually a perfect quality measure
Popularity reflects general interest, not whether the model's training data, license, and limitations fit your specific use case
Stars only apply to datasets, not models
The Hub does not have a star feature
questions.explanation: A widely-starred model can still be the wrong fit — trained on the wrong domain, under a restrictive license, or outdated. The model card, not the star count, is what actually tells you whether it fits.

questions.question: Why should you pin a specific revision (commit) of a Hub repo in production code?
options: Pinning a revision is required by law
Without pinning, a later update to that repo could silently change the weights or config your pipeline loads
Revisions only exist for datasets, not models
Pinning makes the model download faster
questions.explanation: The Hub is git-backed, so a repo can change over time. Pinning a revision means your code always loads the exact same weights and config you tested with, instead of whatever the maintainer pushed most recently.

questions.question: What three kinds of repos does the Hugging Face Hub host, according to this lesson?
options: Only models, nothing else
Models, datasets, and Spaces
Only datasets and licenses
Only Spaces and demos
questions.explanation: The Hub hosts three kinds of repos: models (trained weights and configs), datasets (data files plus loading scripts), and Spaces (small hosted demo apps).

questions.question: What format does a Hugging Face Hub repo id take?
options: A random numeric tracking code
org/name, such as google-bert/bert-base-uncased
Just a single word with no structure
A URL to an external website only
questions.explanation: A repo id follows the org/name format, identifying both the organization or user and the specific repo, such as google-bert/bert-base-uncased.

questions.question: What underlying technology is the Hugging Face Hub built on?
options: A proprietary, closed database with no version history
Git, giving it a commit history like any git repository
A spreadsheet-based storage system
A purely in-memory cache with no persistence
questions.explanation: The Hub is a registry built on git, which is exactly why it maintains a commit history that lets you pin a specific revision of a repo.

questions.question: According to this lesson, what does a model card document about a repo?
options: Only the file size of the model
What the model was trained on, its intended use, known limitations, and its license
Only the programming language used to build it
Nothing useful — model cards are purely decorative
questions.explanation: A model card documents what the model was trained on, its intended use, known limitations, and its license — the essential context for deciding whether to trust and use it.

questions.question: Why does this lesson connect the Hub's models to the transformers course you studied earlier?
options: It doesn't — the Hub is entirely unrelated to the transformers course
The Hub's models are the same BERT and GPT-style architectures from the transformers course, packaged as downloadable, versioned artifacts
The Hub only hosts architectures that predate the transformers course
The transformers course covered a completely different type of model
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly notes that Hub models are the same BERT and GPT-style architectures studied in the transformers course, just packaged as downloadable, versioned artifacts instead of research-paper diagrams.

lessons.title: AutoTokenizer and AutoModel: One Interface, Many Architectures
lessons.description: See how the Auto* classes give you a consistent API across BERT, GPT, and other architectures.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what `AutoTokenizer` and `AutoModel` do and why the same three lines of code work whether you load a BERT encoder or a GPT-style decoder.

sections.title: 🔌 A universal adapter over architectures
sections.content:
In the transformers course, you learned that BERT (encoder-only) and GPT (decoder-only) are architecturally different. The `transformers` library hides that difference behind **Auto classes**: `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo_id)` and `AutoModel.from_pretrained(repo_id)` inspect the repo's config and load the right tokenizer and model class automatically.

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")

inputs = tokenizer("Transformers are everywhere.", return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model(**inputs)
print(outputs.last_hidden_state.shape)  # (batch, seq_len, hidden_size)
```

sections.title: 🎯 Task-specific heads
sections.content:
`AutoModel` returns raw hidden states — useful for embeddings, but not a classification directly. Task-specific classes like `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` or `AutoModelForCausalLM` attach the right head on top, the same head-on-top-of-backbone pattern from the transfer learning lesson in the deep learning course.

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification

clf_model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    "bert-base-uncased", num_labels=2
)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Mixing tokenizer and model from different repos.** A tokenizer must match the exact model it was trained with — vocabularies and special tokens differ between checkpoints.

**Using `AutoModel` when you need a task head.** Raw hidden states aren't classification logits; pick the right `AutoModelFor...` class for your task.

**Forgetting `return_tensors`.** Without it, the tokenizer returns plain Python lists, not the tensors your model's framework expects.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of using `AutoTokenizer` and `AutoModel` instead of architecture-specific classes?
options: They only work with BERT and no other architecture
They provide one consistent API that automatically loads the correct tokenizer/model class based on the repo's config, whether it's BERT, GPT, or another architecture
They are faster than any other way to load a model
They eliminate the need for a tokenizer entirely
questions.explanation: The whole point of the Auto* classes is architectural abstraction: the same `from_pretrained(repo_id)` call works across very different underlying architectures because it reads the repo's config to pick the right class.

questions.question: Why must a tokenizer and model always come from the same repo (or be explicitly compatible)?
options: It's just a coding convention with no real effect
The tokenizer's vocabulary and special tokens must match exactly what the model was trained with, or the token ids fed into the model become meaningless
Tokenizers and models are always interchangeable regardless of source
Only GPT-style models require matching tokenizers
questions.explanation: A model was trained to associate specific token ids with specific meanings. Using a mismatched tokenizer produces different ids for the same text, which the model was never trained to interpret correctly.

questions.question: When should you use `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` instead of plain `AutoModel`?
options: Never — they are identical
When you need a classification head attached on top of the backbone, rather than raw hidden states
Only when working with images, not text
Only when using GPT-style models
questions.explanation: `AutoModel` returns raw hidden states useful for embeddings or custom heads. `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` attaches an actual classification head on top, so its output is ready-to-use logits for a labeled task.

questions.question: What problem do the Auto* classes solve, according to this lesson?
options: They make training run faster on any hardware
They hide the architectural differences between models like BERT and GPT behind one consistent loading API
They eliminate the need for a tokenizer entirely
They replace the need for a model card
questions.explanation: Auto classes like AutoTokenizer and AutoModel provide one consistent API that automatically loads the correct tokenizer/model class regardless of the underlying architecture, hiding differences like BERT's encoder vs. GPT's decoder.

questions.question: What does `AutoModel` return, as opposed to a task-specific class like `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`?
options: Ready-to-use classification logits
Raw hidden states, without a task-specific head attached
A fully trained classifier with no further setup needed
Nothing — AutoModel cannot be used to load a model
questions.explanation: AutoModel returns raw hidden states, useful for embeddings but not directly usable for classification — a task-specific class like AutoModelForSequenceClassification attaches the actual task head on top.

questions.question: What pattern from the deep learning course does attaching a task-specific head to a backbone echo?
options: The vanishing gradient problem
The transfer learning pattern of a head-on-top-of-backbone
The concept of a loss function
Data augmentation
questions.explanation: Attaching a task-specific head (like AutoModelForSequenceClassification) on top of a pretrained backbone is the same head-on-top-of-backbone pattern from the transfer learning lesson in the deep learning course.

questions.question: What happens if you use a tokenizer from one repo with a model from a different, incompatible repo?
options: Nothing goes wrong — tokenizers and models are always interchangeable
The token ids fed into the model become meaningless, since vocabularies and special tokens differ between checkpoints
The model automatically detects and fixes the mismatch
This combination always runs faster than using matching tokenizer and model
questions.explanation: A tokenizer must match the exact model it was trained with — mixing mismatched tokenizer and model produces token ids that don't correspond to what the model actually learned.

questions.question: What does forgetting `return_tensors` when calling a tokenizer typically cause?
options: The tokenizer crashes and returns nothing
The tokenizer returns plain Python lists instead of the tensors your model's framework expects
It automatically converts output to the correct tensor format regardless
It has no effect on the tokenizer's output format
questions.explanation: Without specifying return_tensors, the tokenizer returns plain Python lists rather than the tensor format (like PyTorch tensors) that the model expects as input.

lessons.title: Pipelines: The Fast Path to a Working Model
lessons.description: Use the pipeline() helper to go from raw text to results in one line, and know when to graduate past it.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can use `pipeline()` to quickly try a task, and explain why production systems usually move beyond it.

sections.title: ⚡ One line, many tasks
sections.content:
`pipeline()` bundles a tokenizer, a model, and the pre/post-processing for a specific task into a single callable. It is the fastest way to check whether an idea works at all.

```python
from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
result = classifier("This lesson is actually pretty clear.")
print(result)  # [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.999...}]

summarizer = pipeline("summarization")
generator = pipeline("text-generation", model="gpt2")
```

sections.title: 🔬 Prototype vs. production
sections.content: Pipelines default to a preset model and hide all the tokenizer/model wiring — great for a prototype, but you lose fine control over batching, device placement, and the exact checkpoint used. Production systems usually load the `AutoTokenizer`/`AutoModel` pair explicitly once, batch inputs, and reuse the loaded model across many requests instead of rebuilding a pipeline per call.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Rebuilding a pipeline inside a request loop.** Loading a model is expensive; build it once and reuse it.

**Trusting the default model for a serious task.** Pipelines pick a reasonable default checkpoint, but you should pin one explicitly (`pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model="...")`) once you move past prototyping.

**Never graduating past the pipeline.** It hides the tokenizer/model split, which becomes limiting the moment you need custom batching or a fine-tuned checkpoint.

questions.question: What does `pipeline()` bundle together into a single callable?
options: Only the model weights, with no tokenizer
A tokenizer, a model, and the task-specific pre/post-processing needed to go from raw input to a usable result
A full training loop
A dataset loader only
questions.explanation: A pipeline wraps the tokenizer, the model, and the pre/post-processing logic for a specific task (like sentiment analysis or summarization) so you can call it directly on raw text.

questions.question: Why is rebuilding a pipeline inside a request-handling loop a performance mistake?
options: It isn't a mistake — pipelines are free to create
Loading a model's weights is expensive, so recreating the pipeline per request repeats that expensive load unnecessarily
Pipelines can only be created once per program, ever
It causes a licensing violation
questions.explanation: Model loading is the expensive part. Build the pipeline (or the tokenizer/model pair) once at startup and reuse it across many calls, rather than reloading weights on every request.

questions.question: Why might a production system use `AutoTokenizer`/`AutoModel` directly instead of `pipeline()`?
options: Because pipelines cannot run on GPUs
Because direct control over batching, device placement, and the exact checkpoint used matters more than convenience once you're past prototyping
Because pipelines only work for image tasks
Because AutoTokenizer and pipeline() are actually the same thing
questions.explanation: Pipelines optimize for quick prototyping by hiding details. Production systems often need to control batching, device placement, and exact checkpoints precisely, which means working with the tokenizer and model directly.

questions.question: What does `pipeline()` bundle into a single callable, according to this lesson?
options: Only a dataset with no model
A tokenizer, a model, and the pre/post-processing needed for a specific task
A full training loop with no inference capability
Only a license checker
questions.explanation: pipeline() bundles a tokenizer, a model, and the task-specific pre/post-processing into one callable, letting you go from raw text to results in a single line.

questions.question: According to this lesson, what is pipeline() best suited for?
options: Large-scale production deployment with full control over batching
Quickly checking whether an idea works at all — fast prototyping
Replacing the need for any model card review
Training a model from scratch
questions.explanation: The lesson describes pipeline() as the fastest way to check whether an idea works at all — ideal for prototyping, though production systems usually move beyond it.

questions.question: What do you lose by relying on `pipeline()`'s default settings rather than explicit AutoTokenizer/AutoModel loading?
options: Nothing is lost; the two approaches are functionally identical in every respect
Fine control over batching, device placement, and the exact checkpoint used
The ability to process any text at all
The ability to use more than one task at a time
questions.explanation: Pipelines hide the tokenizer/model wiring for convenience, but this means losing fine control over batching, device placement, and the exact checkpoint used — control that production systems typically need.

questions.question: Why is rebuilding a pipeline inside a request-handling loop considered a mistake?
options: It isn't a mistake — pipelines cost nothing to create repeatedly
Loading a model's weights is expensive, so recreating the pipeline per request repeats that expensive load unnecessarily
Pipelines can only be built once per entire program execution
It causes a licensing violation each time
questions.explanation: Since loading a model is the expensive part, rebuilding the pipeline (and reloading the model) on every request wastes that cost repeatedly instead of loading once and reusing it.

questions.question: What does the lesson recommend once you move past prototyping with a pipeline for a serious task?
options: Never using any pipeline again for any purpose
Pinning an explicit model rather than relying on the pipeline's default checkpoint
Deleting the pipeline's tokenizer entirely
Switching to a completely different, unrelated task
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends pinning an explicit model (e.g., pipeline('sentiment-analysis', model='...')) once you move past prototyping, rather than trusting the pipeline's default checkpoint for serious work.

lessons.title: Reading Model Cards and Licenses
lessons.description: Learn what to check in a model card before you rely on a model for real work.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can list the key things to check in a model card before using a model in a project.

sections.title: 📋 What a good model card tells you
sections.content:
A model card typically documents: the **training data** (what the model has and hasn't seen), **intended use** (what tasks it was built for), **limitations and biases** (known failure modes), and the **license** (what you're legally allowed to do with it).

This matters just as much as accuracy — a model trained mostly on English news text may perform far worse on informal text in another language, even if its benchmark numbers look impressive.

sections.title: ⚖️ Licenses are not all equal
sections.content:
Some models use permissive licenses (Apache 2.0, MIT); others are research-only, require attribution, or restrict commercial use. Two models that look interchangeable technically can be completely different legally.

```python
# Not code you run, but a decision you should make explicitly:
# Can I use this model in a commercial product?
# Do I need to credit the model in my product?
# Are there usage restrictions (e.g. no use in specific domains)?
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming all open-weights models are free to use commercially.** "Open weights" and "open license" are not the same thing.

**Skipping the limitations section.** A model card's documented failure modes are exactly the edge cases your users will hit first.

**Not checking training data recency.** A model with a training cutoff can be confidently wrong about anything newer.

questions.question: Why is checking the license of a model just as important as checking its accuracy?
options: Licenses don't actually matter for machine learning models
A model can be technically excellent but legally restricted from the use you have in mind, such as commercial deployment
All models on the Hub share the same license
Licenses only apply to datasets, not models
questions.explanation: Two models can perform similarly well but carry very different licenses — one permissive, one restricted to research or requiring specific attribution. Skipping this check can create legal exposure later.

questions.question: What does "open weights" mean, and how does it differ from "open license"?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
"Open weights" means the trained parameters are downloadable; that does not automatically mean the license permits any use you want, including commercial use
"Open weights" refers only to datasets
Open weights models have no license at all
questions.explanation: A model can have publicly downloadable weights (open weights) while still being governed by a license that restricts commercial use or certain applications — the two are independent facts you need to check separately.

questions.question: Why does a model's training data recency matter when you're evaluating it for a task?
options: It never matters — models are timeless
A model can only reflect knowledge up to its training cutoff, so it may be confidently wrong about anything that happened or changed afterward
Recency only matters for image models
Newer training data always makes a model worse
questions.explanation: Like any model trained on a snapshot of data, an HF model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff. For tasks involving recent information, this is a real limitation you should check for before relying on it.

questions.question: What four things does a good model card typically document, according to this lesson?
options: Only the model's file size and download count
Training data, intended use, limitations and biases, and the license
Only the programming language and framework version
Only the number of GitHub stars
questions.explanation: A good model card documents training data, intended use, limitations and biases, and the license — information that matters just as much as raw accuracy numbers.

questions.question: Why can two models with similarly impressive benchmark numbers still perform very differently in practice?
options: Benchmark numbers always fully predict real-world performance
A model's training data might not match your actual use case, such as informal text or a different language than what it was trained on
This never actually happens in practice
Benchmark numbers are randomly generated and meaningless
questions.explanation: A model trained mostly on one kind of text (like English news) may perform far worse on different text (like informal language or another language), even with strong benchmark numbers — training data fit matters as much as accuracy.

questions.question: What is the key distinction this lesson draws between 'open weights' and 'open license'?
options: They are exactly the same thing
Open weights means the trained parameters are downloadable, which doesn't automatically mean the license permits any use, including commercial use
Open license means the weights cannot be downloaded at all
Neither term has any real meaning in practice
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that downloadable weights (open weights) and a license permitting your intended use (open license) are independent facts — a model can have one without the other.

questions.question: Why does a model's training data cutoff date matter when evaluating it for a task?
options: Training data recency has no bearing on model quality
A model can only reflect knowledge up to its training cutoff, so it may be confidently wrong about anything that happened or changed afterward
Older training data always makes a model more accurate
Cutoff dates only apply to image models, never text models
questions.explanation: Since a model's knowledge is fixed at its training cutoff, it can be confidently wrong about more recent developments — a real limitation to check before relying on it for time-sensitive information.

questions.question: According to this lesson, why is skipping a model card's limitations section a mistake?
options: Limitations sections never contain useful information
The documented failure modes are exactly the edge cases your users are likely to encounter first
Limitations sections are purely legal boilerplate with no practical value
Skipping it has no consequence since limitations never actually occur
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that a model card's documented limitations are precisely the failure modes users will run into in practice, making this section directly relevant rather than something to skip.
